triage_reasoning: CD63 is a tetraspanin that resides predominantly on lysosomal/late endosomal/multivesicular body membranes and melanosomes. It reaches the plasma membrane via regulated lysosomal exocytosis/degranulation in specific cell types - most notably activated platelets (alpha-granule/dense-granule release), mast cells, basophils, and NK cells - where surface CD63 is a well-documented activation marker measured by flow cytometry on intact cells. It is also enriched on exosome membranes. Baseline localization in most cells is intracellular endomembrane, but the regulated surface appearance is well-documented and gene-specific (not generic class analogy), fitting lysosomal_exocytosis rather than constitutive surface residence.

executive_summary.one_paragraph: CD63 is state-dependently surface-accessible as a four-pass tetraspanin whose plasma membrane pool is driven by lysosomal exocytosis upon immune-cell activation. Direct multi-method support: live-cell flow cytometry with CRISPR-KO controls on HEK293T cells (a1_evi_05, a1_evi_06), live-cell flow on primary human eosinophils, basophils, and neutrophils (a1_evi_12, a1_evi_13, a1_evi_15), and KO-validated non-permeabilized confocal imaging with nanobody 2E-Nb (a1_evi_22). Surface presence is highly state-modulated: resting cells retain CD63 predominantly in lysosomes/MVBs (a2_evi_22), while degranulation in mast cells, eosinophils, basophils, and platelets drives robust surface translocation (a2_evi_05, a2_evi_08, a2_evi_13). Moderate epitope masking via heavy EC2 glycosylation and TEM partner occlusion is the principal binder-engineering caveat (a1_evi_03, a1_evi_04); shed and secreted forms are absent, ruling out decoy concerns.
executive_summary.accessibility_context_summary: Surface-accessible on activated/degranulating immune cells (mast cells, eosinophils, basophils, platelets, neutrophils) and macrophages in inflammatory or tumor contexts; predominantly intracellular (lysosomal/MVB) in resting cells across most tissues.

filters.expression_level_rationale: CD63 is broadly expressed at moderate levels across immune cells, mesenchymal stem cells, hepatocytes, and epithelial tissues; expression is high in activated granulocytes and limbal stem cells (a2_evi_02, a2_evi_05) but moderate at baseline in most cell types (a2_evi_04, a2_evi_23).
filters.expression_breadth_rationale: CD63 was excluded from tissue-specific surface target screens due to non-tissue-specific expression across multiple human tissues (a2_evi_04); expression is documented in blood, lung, liver, brain, pancreas, cornea, adipose, and skeletal muscle (a2_evi_23, a2_evi_24).
filters.surface_specificity_rationale: The dominant resting compartment is lysosomal/MVB (a2_evi_22, a1_evi_28); plasma membrane pool is activation-induced via lysosomal exocytosis in immune cells (a2_evi_05, a2_evi_08), making the protein mostly intracellular at baseline with a state-conditional surface fraction.
filters.has_known_ligand_rationale: TIMP1 is a validated endogenous binding partner that engages CD63 (with β1-integrin) on macrophage surfaces to activate AKT/mTOR signaling (a2_evi_17); this constitutes a documented physiological ligand-receptor interaction.
filters.low_endogenous_expression_rationale: CD63 is broadly expressed at moderate levels across immune cells, mesenchymal stem cells, hepatocytes, and epithelial tissues; expression is high in activated granulocytes and limbal stem cells (a2_evi_02, a2_evi_05) but moderate at baseline in most cell types (a2_evi_04, a2_evi_23).
filters.overexpression_surface_localization_obse: No method observation pairs an overexpression/mixed expression system with a direct or supportive surface-accessibility readout.

surface_evidence.grade_rationale: Multiple independent direct-surface-accessibility method types confirm CD63 plasma membrane exposure. (1) Live-cell flow cytometry on HEK293T cells with CRISPR-KO negative controls (CD63-KO signal abolished) establishes surface accessibility with genetic antibody validation (a1_evi_05, a1_evi_06). (2) Live-cell flow on primary human eosinophils from asthma patients directly confirms surface CD63 (a1_evi_12). (3) Live-cell flow on primary human basophils upon activation (a1_evi_13). (4) Live-cell flow on primary human neutrophils in a clinical cardiac surgery cohort (a1_evi_15). (5) Non-permeabilized confocal IF with nanobody 2E-Nb on WT vs CD63-KO HEK293T cells, KO-validated (a1_evi_22). These span two distinct direct method classes (live-cell flow and nonperm IF) across multiple human primary cell types and cell lines, with CRISPR-KO controls anchoring antibody specificity. Surface appearance is state-conditional (lysosomal exocytosis upon activation in granulocytes/platelets) but constitutive in HEK293T. EV-surface claims (a1_evi_18–24) and ligand-engagement claims (a1_evi_25, a1_evi_26) were excluded. Graded direct_multi_method.

subcellular_localization.rationale: CD63 is a canonical late-endosomal/lysosomal tetraspanin. Permeabilized IF in hUCMSCs shows predominant localization to multivesicular bodies (MVBs), the primary EV precursor compartment (a2_evi_22). Lysosomal degradation controls CD63 protein abundance in HCC cells (a2_evi_21). Surface pool is activation-induced in immune cells (a2_evi_05, a2_evi_08, a2_evi_13), confirming endosome as the dominant resting compartment.

dual_localization.rationale: Non-permeabilized flow cytometry on intact mast cells (a2_evi_05, a2_evi_12), eosinophils (a2_evi_08, a2_evi_09), basophils (a2_evi_10, a2_evi_11), platelets (a2_evi_13), neutrophils (a2_evi_14), macrophages (a2_evi_16, a2_evi_17), and T cells (a2_evi_18) confirms activation-induced surface translocation from intracellular granules.

Lysosomal acidification blockade with bafilomycin A1 rescues CD63 protein levels in HCC cells (a2_evi_21), and NPC patient EVs are enriched for endolysosomal CD63/LAMP1 (a2_evi_25), consistent with CD63 cycling through the lysosomal compartment.

CD63 is a canonical EV/exosome marker enriched on secreted vesicles from multiple cell types including hUCMSCs, astrocytes, and metabolic cells (a2_evi_20, a2_evi_22, a2_evi_23, a2_evi_25). Elevated alveolar CD63 in COPD correlates with increased BAL exosome number (a2_evi_19).

accessibility_modulation.change: MRGPRX2-mediated activation induces degranulation with significant rise in CD63 surface expression on LAD2 mast cells, confirming translocation of CD63 from intracellular granules to the plasma membrane.
accessibility_modulation.accessibility_implication: CD63 becomes substantially more accessible to extracellular binders on mast cell surface upon activation/degranulation; resting mast cells present low surface CD63.

accessibility_modulation.change: Upon degranulation, CD63 translocates from intracellular granules to the eosinophil cell surface; resting eosinophils have low surface CD63 while activated/degranulating eosinophils show elevated surface CD63.
accessibility_modulation.accessibility_implication: CD63 is accessible to extracellular binders on eosinophils primarily in the activated/degranulating state; resting eosinophils present minimal surface CD63.

accessibility_modulation.modulating_state: alpha-gal antigen-stimulated RBL SX-38 mast cells
accessibility_modulation.change: Alpha-gal antigen stimulation increases CD63+ cell percentage ~3-fold compared to control-sensitized cells, confirming activation-induced surface translocation of CD63 in mast cells.
accessibility_modulation.accessibility_implication: Antigen stimulation markedly increases CD63 surface accessibility on mast cells, enabling extracellular targeting in activated states.

accessibility_modulation.change: During activation and degranulation, basophils express CD63 on their surface as a unique activation marker; CD63 surface expression is a well-established readout of basophil degranulation state.
accessibility_modulation.accessibility_implication: CD63 surface accessibility on basophils is state-dependent, appearing upon activation/degranulation and enabling extracellular targeting in activated basophils.

accessibility_modulation.modulating_state: M2-polarized tumor-associated macrophages in colorectal cancer hepatic pre-metastatic niche
accessibility_modulation.change: TIMP1 from CRC engages CD63 on macrophage surface (with β1-integrin), activating AKT/mTOR and stabilizing M2 phenotype; CD63 surface accessibility on macrophages is functionally relevant in the tumor microenvironment.
accessibility_modulation.accessibility_implication: CD63 is surface-accessible on tumor-associated macrophages in the CRC liver metastasis niche, making it a potential target in the tumor microenvironment.

accessibility_modulation.modulating_state: HIV-exposed macrophages following contact with HIV-infected T cells
accessibility_modulation.change: HIV-exposed macrophages upregulate tetraspanins including CD63 on their surface alongside ICAM-1/LFA-1, indicating infection-induced increase in surface CD63 on macrophages.
accessibility_modulation.accessibility_implication: HIV exposure increases CD63 surface accessibility on macrophages, potentially enabling extracellular targeting in HIV infection contexts.

accessibility_modulation.modulating_state: platelets from T2DM mice (high-fat diet + STZ model)
accessibility_modulation.change: Flow cytometry reveals elevated platelet surface CD63 (alongside CD62P and CD40L) in T2DM mice compared to healthy controls; DHM treatment reduces surface CD63, demonstrating pharmacological reversibility.
accessibility_modulation.accessibility_implication: CD63 is more accessible on platelet surfaces in diabetic disease state, potentially enabling targeting of activated platelets in T2DM.

accessibility_modulation.change: CD63 is identified as a conserved T-cell host factor supporting ACE2-independent SARS-CoV-2 (Omicron) entry in T lymphocytes, establishing surface CD63 as functionally relevant in viral infection context.
accessibility_modulation.accessibility_implication: CD63 surface accessibility on T lymphocytes is functionally exploited by SARS-CoV-2 Omicron for ACE2-independent entry, indicating surface exposure in this infection context.

accessibility_modulation.change: CD63 predominantly localizes to multivesicular bodies (MVBs/late endosomes/lysosomes) in hUCMSCs, with only a minor plasma membrane pool; intracellular MVB localization is the dominant compartment in this cell type.
accessibility_modulation.accessibility_implication: In mesenchymal stem cells, the majority of CD63 is intracellular (MVB/lysosomal), limiting surface accessibility; extracellular binders will access only the minor plasma membrane fraction.

accessibility_modulation.change: In HCC cells, CD63 protein abundance is controlled by lysosomal/autophagy-dependent degradation; ANXA2 loss reduces CD63 protein without affecting mRNA, and lysosomal acidification blockade rescues CD63 levels, indicating PTM/degradation-dependent regulation of CD63 availability.
accessibility_modulation.accessibility_implication: CD63 surface and exosomal availability in HCC cells is regulated post-translationally via lysosomal turnover; perturbations to lysosomal function alter the pool available for surface presentation.

accessibility_modulation.change: CD63 is predominantly expressed in the basal epithelial cells of the limbus (limbal stem cells) in human ocular surface tissue, with strong limbal expression and restricted distribution compared to central cornea.
accessibility_modulation.accessibility_implication: CD63 surface accessibility is enriched in limbal basal epithelial/stem cell compartment; central corneal epithelium presents lower CD63, limiting binder access to the limbal niche.

biological_context.grade_rationale: All four A2 axes are well-populated from independent sources. Expression is mapped across ≥10 cell types/tissues (mast cells, eosinophils, basophils, platelets, neutrophils, macrophages, T cells, LSCs, astrocytes, HCC, fibroblasts, pancreas, brain). Subcellular localization is pinned to MVBs/lysosomes (a2_evi_22) with plasma-membrane translocation on degranulation. Anatomical accessibility spans ocular surface, blood, lung, liver, brain. Modulation is documented across multiple activation states, disease states, and pharmacological interventions. Picture is internally coherent: intracellular-dominant baseline with state-dependent surface translocation.

co_receptor_requirements.rationale: CD63 is a tetraspanin that traffics independently to the plasma membrane via lysosomal exocytosis (a1_evi_11, a2_evi_08). While it associates with integrins and other proteins in TEMs (a1_evi_04), no ledger entry documents that any partner is required for CD63 to reach the cell surface. Surface expression is confirmed on multiple cell types without partner co-dependency (a1_evi_05, a1_evi_10).

shed_form.rationale: No relevant data in the ledger. No ledger entry documents proteolytic release of the CD63 ectodomain by a sheddase or detection of soluble CD63 in supernatant or serum.

secreted_form.rationale: No relevant data in the ledger for a free soluble CD63 species. EV-associated CD63 is documented extensively (a1_evi_18, a1_evi_19, a1_evi_23) but EV-enclosed protein is not a circulating decoy. No soluble splice isoform or shed ectodomain of CD63 itself is reported in the ledger.

restricted_subdomain.rationale: CD63 surface expression is detected broadly across multiple non-polarized cell types including HEK293T, platelets, basophils, eosinophils, neutrophils, mast cells, macrophages, and T cells by flow cytometry on intact cells (a1_evi_05, a1_evi_10, a1_evi_12, a1_evi_13, a1_evi_15, a2_evi_09). No ledger entry documents restriction to an apical, junctional, or other polarized subdomain.

ecd_size_assessment.rationale: ECD length 114 residues (60-199) -> moderate; computed deterministically from DeepTMHMM topology.

epitope_masking.rationale: Two masking axes are ledger-supported. (1) Glycan: the EC2 loop of CD63 is heavily glycosylated at N130, N150, N172; glycopeptides from this loop are otherwise inaccessible with standard methods (a1_evi_03), indicating glycan shielding of epitopes. (2) Partner: CD63 constitutively associates with integrins and other proteins in tetraspanin-enriched microdomains (TEMs) on intact cell membranes, which may occlude the EC2 epitope (a1_evi_04). Homo-oligomerization is not ledger-supported (deterministic prior is false; no ledger entry documents CD63 homodimerization burying ECD surface).

evidence.claim: CD63 belongs to the tetraspanin superfamily, which is canonically defined by four transmembrane domains (TM1-TM4), a small extracellular loop (EC1), a large extracellular loop (EC2), and short intracellular N- and C-termini. This topology places the large EC2 loop (residues ~103-203 in CD63) on the extracellular face and both termini in the cytoplasm, consistent with DeepTMHMM predictions.

spans.quote: Tetraspanins are a superfamily of transmembrane proteins, consisting of 33 members in humans, that are classically characterised by four transmembrane domains (TM1‐TM4), a small extracellular loop (EC1), a large extracellular loop (EC2), along with short intracellular N‐ and C‐termini [ 1 ].

evidence.claim: CD63 is described as an EV tetraspanin with a nanobody insertion site in the extracellular loop between the third and fourth transmembrane domains, confirming the 4-TM topology with an accessible extracellular loop (EC2) on the outer leaflet. This topology supports ECD accessibility for antibody and nanobody binding.

spans.quote: To establish a CD3 targeting EV platform for CAR transgene delivery, we developed a CD3ε Nb‐CD63 chimeric construct, which consists of the EV tetraspanin protein CD63, with a CD3ε Nb inserted into the extracellular loop between the third and fourth transmembrane domains (Figure 1A ).

evidence.claim: CD63 is described as having a large extracellular loop that is highly glycosylated, with glycopeptides from this loop being otherwise inaccessible with standard methods. This highlights that heavy glycosylation of the EC2 loop (N130, N150, N172) may mask epitopes and reduce antibody accessibility on the native protein surface.

spans.quote: These glycopeptides, derived from the large extracellular loop of the highly glycosylated CD63, illustrate the type of targets that are otherwise inaccessible with current methods but can be readily obtained using ENCOREP.

evidence.claim: Tetraspanins including CD63 associate with integrins, proteoglycans, and immunoglobulin superfamily members to form tetraspanin-enriched microdomains (TEMs). This partner-protein association may mask the CD63 EC2 epitope in the context of intact cell membranes, representing an epitope-masking risk for antibody-based surface detection.

spans.quote: A key characteristic of tetraspanins is their ability to associate with various membrane proteins, including integrins, proteoglycans and immunoglobulin superfamily members [ 3 , 4 ], to form molecular complexes known as tetraspanin‐enriched microdomains (TEMs) [ 5 ].

evidence.claim: Flow cytometry on live HEK293T wild-type cells detected CD63 on the cell surface (positive staining for CD9, CD63, and CD81). This is a direct surface-accessibility readout on intact, non-permeabilized cells using APC-conjugated antibodies, confirming that CD63 is accessible at the plasma membrane of HEK293T cells under basal conditions.

spans.quote: Flow cytometric analysis showed that HEK293T WT cells and WT‐EVs were positive for CD9, CD63, and CD81 on their surface (Figure 2B,C ).

evidence.claim: Flow cytometry on CD63-knockout (CRISPR/Cas9) HEK293T cells showed complete absence of CD63 surface staining, confirming antibody specificity via genetic KO validation. PanKO cells (CD9/CD63/CD81 triple KO) also lacked all three tetraspanin signals. This KO-validation anchors the surface-detection antibody specificity.

spans.quote: In contrast, PanKO cells (lacking the tetraspanins CD9, CD63, and CD81) showed no detectable staining for CD9, CD63, or CD81, confirming the knockout efficiency; this absence of tetraspanin expression was also observed in PanKO‐derived EVs, which lacked detectable levels of these markers (Figures 2B,C and S1D).

evidence.claim: HeLa CD63-KO cells were generated by CRISPR/Cas9 (one sub-clone from bulk population after 2 rounds of sorting, as described in Palmulli et al. 2024). These KO cells serve as a validated negative control for CD63 surface detection by flow cytometry and single-vesicle imaging, anchoring antibody specificity for CD63 surface assays.

evidence.claim: Flow cytometry on live platelets from a T2DM mouse model detected CD63 surface expression (alongside CD62P and CD40L). DHM treatment significantly reduced platelet surface CD63 expression. This is a direct surface-accessibility readout on intact, non-permeabilized platelets, confirming regulated surface translocation of CD63 upon platelet activation.

spans.quote: A T2DM mouse model was established by feeding a high-fat diet (HFD) combined with streptozotocin (STZ) injection, followed by dietary supplementation with DHM (500 or 1000 mg kg<sup>-1</sup> in diets) for eight weeks. Flow cytometric analysis revealed that DHM significantly reduced platelet surface expression of CD62P, CD63, and CD40 ligands, decreased integrin αIIbβ3 activation, and suppressed intraplatelet reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. The exaggerated platelet aggregation and ATP secretion induced by thrombin and collagen were also markedly attenuated.

evidence.claim: Upon degranulation, CD63 translocates to the cell surface of eosinophils, making it a reliable surrogate marker for eosinophil activation in allergic and inflammatory settings. This review assertion describes the regulated surface translocation mechanism (lysosomal exocytosis) that underlies CD63 plasma membrane appearance.

spans.quote: Upon degranulation, CD63 translocates to the cell surface, making it a reliable surrogate marker for eosinophil activation in various allergic and inflammatory settings 3 .

spans.quote: Immunostaining of human corneal tissue demonstrated strong CD63 expression localized to the limbal region.

evidence.claim: Single-particle interferometric reflectance imaging sensing (SP-IRIS) detected CD63 expression on a population of 40-45 nm vesicles from bovine colostrum-derived extracellular vesicles, alongside CD9. This is a direct single-particle surface-marker detection method on intact vesicles, confirming CD63 is accessible on the outer surface of small EVs.

spans.quote: Dynamic light scattering indicated an average BCEV diameter of 127.3 ± 9.5 nm, whereas single-particle interferometric reflectance imaging sensing revealed a smaller population of 40- to 45-nm vesicles expressing CD9 and CD63.

evidence.claim: ELISA-based EV surface marker detection confirmed CD63 expression on EVs from human gingival fibroblasts (hGFs-MVs), with CD63 showing higher expression than CD9 and CD81. This is a direct surface-accessibility readout on intact vesicles using antibody-based ELISA, confirming CD63 is present on the outer surface of EVs.

spans.quote: All common EV surface markers—CD9, CD63, and CD81–were detected, with CD63 showing higher expression.

evidence.claim: Flow-induced dispersion analysis (FIDA) was used to characterize EV-antibody interactions using anti-CD63 antibodies on three EV sources: EVs from HEK cells expressing CD63-eGFP, CD63-NeonGreen-Fc domain (CD63-NG-Fc), and ciMSC-derived EVs. This method directly measures antibody binding to CD63 on the outer surface of intact vesicles, confirming ECD accessibility.

spans.quote: Here, FIDA was applied to characterize EV-antibody interactions using anti-CD63 antibodies across three EV sources: EVs from genetically engineered HEK cells expressing CD63-eGFP or CD63-NeonGreen-Fc domain (CD63-NG-Fc), and EVs from clonally expanded immortalized mesenchymal stromal cells (ciMSCs).

evidence.claim: FIDA quantified CD63-binding EC50 values: 1.9×10^8 particles/mL for CD63-eGFP EVs and 8.4×10^8 to 2.4×10^9 particles/mL for ciMSC EVs, indicating higher epitope abundance in engineered vesicles vs. endogenous EVs. This quantitative surface-accessibility measurement confirms CD63 ECD is accessible on native EV surfaces, though at lower epitope density than overexpressed constructs.

spans.quote: CD63-binding EC<sub>50 </sub>values were 1.9 × 10<sup>8</sup> particles/mL for CD63-eGFP EVs and 8.4 × 10<sup>8</sup> to 2.4 × 10<sup>9</sup> particles/mL for ciMSC EVs, indicating higher epitope abundance in engineered vesicles.

evidence.claim: Confocal microscopy verified co-localization of nanobody 2E-Nb with CD63 in wild-type H293T cells but not in CD63-knockout H293T cells, confirming target specificity. This paired WT/KO validation by immunofluorescence on intact cells is a direct surface-accessibility readout and a methodological validation of the 2E-Nb binder.

spans.quote: Confocal microscopy verified the co-localization of 2E-Nb with CD63 in wild-type but not CD63-knockout H293T cells, confirming target specificity.

evidence.claim: NanoFCM analysis demonstrated that nanobody 2E-Nb effectively recognized native exosomal CD63 isolated from H293T cells and mediated efficient fluorescent labeling. This is a direct surface-accessibility readout on native (non-engineered) EVs, confirming CD63 ECD is accessible on the outer surface of endogenous exosomes.

spans.quote: Furthermore, NanoFCM analysis demonstrated that 2E-Nb effectively recognized native exosomal CD63 isolated from H293T cells and mediated efficient fluorescent labeling.

evidence.claim: Nanobody 2E-Nb, identified by phage display against the purified CD63-ECD (residues 105-238), enables precise targeting of CD63 on exosomal membranes and rapid stable exosome surface modification. This therapeutic-grade binder engaging the CD63 ECD on intact exosome surfaces is direct evidence of ECD surface accessibility.

spans.quote: Here, we report a nanobody (2E-Nb) identified by phage display that enables precise targeting of CD63, a tetraspanin highly enriched on exosomal membranes, allowing rapid and stable exosome surface modification.

evidence.claim: TIMP1 engages CD63/β1-integrin on macrophages, activating AKT/mTOR signaling and stabilizing the M2 phenotype. This ligand-receptor engagement on intact macrophage surfaces is direct evidence that CD63 ECD is accessible at the plasma membrane of macrophages for TIMP1 binding.

spans.quote:
Mechanistically, TIMP1 engaged CD63/β1-integrin on macrophages, activating AKT/mTOR signaling and stabilizing the M2 phenotype.

Conclusions

CRC-derived TIMP1 remodels liver macrophages via the CD63/β1-integrin-AKT/mTOR pathway to promote a hepatic pre-metastatic niche.

evidence.claim: CD63 is identified as a conserved T-cell host factor supporting ACE2-independent SARS-CoV-2 entry. This functional engagement of CD63 by SARS-CoV-2 on T-cell surfaces implies CD63 ECD is accessible at the plasma membrane of T cells for viral interaction.

spans.quote:
Background

Severe Omicron cases present profound lymphocytopenia, suggesting variant-specific immune injury.

Results

We identify CD63 as a conserved T-cell host factor supporting ACE2-independent SARS-CoV-2 entry.

evidence.claim: ANXA2 loss reduces CD63 protein levels without a corresponding decrease in CD63 mRNA, accompanied by activation of lysosome/autophagy-associated programs. Bafilomycin A1 (lysosomal acidification inhibitor) restores CD63 levels, indicating lysosome-dependent turnover is the major contributor to CD63 reduction. This post-translational regulation of CD63 protein stability via lysosomal degradation is relevant to surface accessibility: CD63 predominantly resides in lysosomes and its surface pool depends on regulated exocytosis.

spans.quote: ANXA2 loss reduces CD63 protein levels without a corresponding decrease in CD63 mRNA and is accompanied by activation of lysosome/autophagy-associated programs.

evidence.claim: CD63 is predominantly localized to multivesicular bodies (MVBs) in hUCMSCs, as determined by immunofluorescence. This intracellular localization to MVBs (the primary precursors of EVs) is the baseline compartment for CD63, with surface appearance requiring regulated exocytosis. This is a non-surface expression finding that qualifies the surface claim by establishing the dominant intracellular pool.

spans.quote: Given the predominant localization of CD63 to MVBs, which are the primary precursors of EVs, these findings suggest that H89 may modulate EV secretion pathways in hUCMSCs.

evidence.claim: In a screen of the top 50 genes encoding cell surface molecules, CD63 was among 8 identified but was excluded from further analysis due to non-tissue-specific expression pattern. This finding confirms CD63 is recognized as a cell surface molecule but highlights its ubiquitous expression across tissues, which limits its utility as a tissue-specific surface target.

spans.quote: Among the top 50 genes, 8 encode cell surface molecules. 3 out of the 8 genes ( B2M , CD63 , and CD99 ) were excluded due to their non‐tissue specific expression pattern.

evidence.claim: CD63 protein is strongly expressed in the limbal region of human corneal tissue, as shown by immunostaining of primary human corneal sections. Expression is localized to the limbus rather than the central cornea.

spans.quote: Immunostaining of human corneal tissue demonstrated strong CD63 expression localized to the limbal region.

evidence.claim: In human ocular surface tissue, CD63 is predominantly expressed in the basal epithelial cells of the limbus, consistent with its role as a marker of quiescent limbal stem cells (LSCs). This cell-type restriction to basal limbal epithelium distinguishes CD63 from more broadly expressed corneal markers.

assay_context.cell_type_or_line: basal epithelial cells of human limbus

cell_context.cell_type: basal epithelial cells / limbal stem cells

spans.quote: This study identified that mouse corneal Abcb5-positive LSCs express the recently discovered quiescent LSC markers, such as Gpha2 and Cd63, 22 , 23 supporting their quiescent stem cell identity observed in vivo. 10 In humans, CD63 was found to be predominantly expressed in the basal epithelial cells of the limbus .

evidence.claim: RNA-seq analysis of mouse Abcb5-positive limbal stem cells shows elevated Cd63 expression compared to other corneal epithelial cell populations, identifying Cd63 as a marker of quiescent LSCs alongside Gpha2 and Ifitm3.

spans.quote: Additionally, Abcb5-positive LSCs expressed elevated levels of Gpha2 , Ifitm3 , and Cd63 , which have been identified as additional markers of quiescent LSCs. 22 A recent study by Jiang et al. identified high Ifitm1 expression in LSCs and early transient amplifying (eTA) cells and described its role in promoting cell proliferation through the inhibition of Ovol1. 23 Consistent with these findings, our RNA-seq analysis revealed upregulation of Ifitm1 and downregulation of Ovol1 in Abcb5-positive cells (see Fig. 1 D).

evidence.claim: CD63 was identified among the top 50 cell-surface molecule-encoding genes but was excluded from tissue-specific surface targets due to its non-tissue-specific expression pattern, indicating broad/ubiquitous expression across tissues rather than restricted expression.

spans.quote: Among the top 50 genes, 8 encode cell surface molecules. 3 out of the 8 genes ( B2M , CD63 , and CD99 ) were excluded due to their non‐tissue specific expression pattern.

evidence.claim: In LAD2 mast cells, MRGPRX2-mediated activation induces degranulation accompanied by a significant rise in CD63 surface expression as measured by flow cytometry on intact cells, confirming activation-induced translocation of CD63 to the mast cell plasma membrane.

spans.quote: Activation-induced degranulation of LAD2 cells was further demonstrated by a significant elevation in the secretion of tryptase, a clinically relevant marker for MC degranulation in the serum ( Figure 1 D, Supplementary Figure S1C ); a rise in CD63 and CD107a on the MC surface assessed by flow cytometry ( Figure 1 E,F, Supplementary Figure S1D ), and an increase in phosphorylated ERK as demonstrated by Western blot ( Figure 1 G).

evidence.claim: CD63 cell surface expression on mast cells is a readout of degranulation and is modulated by oat extract exposure, which reduces surface CD63 levels. This confirms that CD63 surface levels on mast cells are activation-state dependent and can be pharmacologically modulated.

spans.quote: Exposure to oat extract resulted in a significant reduction in mast cell degranulation for all three ligands, as assessed by the release of β-hexosaminidase, tryptase, cell surface expression of CD63 and CD107a, and phosphorylation of ERK.

evidence.claim: CD63 is a tetraspanin commonly associated with the activation and degranulation of eosinophils, particularly in response to IgE-mediated stimuli. It is expressed in eosinophils and serves as a reliable surrogate marker for eosinophil activation in allergic and inflammatory settings.

spans.quote: CD63 is a tetraspanin commonly associated with the activation and degranulation of eosinophils, particularly in response to IgE-mediated stimuli.

evidence.claim: Upon degranulation, CD63 translocates from intracellular granules to the eosinophil cell surface, making it a reliable surrogate marker for eosinophil activation. Baseline (resting) eosinophils have low surface CD63; activated/degranulating eosinophils show elevated surface CD63.

spans.quote: Upon degranulation, CD63 translocates to the cell surface, making it a reliable surrogate marker for eosinophil activation in various allergic and inflammatory settings 3 .

evidence.claim: CD63 surface expression is quantified by flow cytometry on circulating eosinophils from patients with hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES), establishing CD63 as a measurable surface marker on primary human eosinophils in a disease context.

spans.quote:
Surface expression of various eosinophil markers, including CD69, CD62L, CD66b, CD107a, CD107b, CD63, CCR3, CXCR4, CD101, and CD274, were quantified in whole blood by flow cytometry.

Results

Absolute eosinophil counts were significantly elevated in symptomatic patients being treated for HES compared to asymptomatic patients being treated for HES.

evidence.claim: During activation and degranulation, basophils express CD63 on their surface as a unique activation marker. CD63 surface expression on basophils is a well-established readout of degranulation state.

spans.quote: During activation and degranulation, basophils expressed unique surface markers such as CD63 and CD203c.

evidence.claim: CD63 surface expression on blood basophils is measured by flow cytometry at baseline and after 12 weeks of omalizumab treatment in patients with moderate-to-severe allergic rhinitis, demonstrating that CD63 is a quantifiable surface marker on primary human basophils in allergic disease and that its expression is modulated by anti-IgE therapy.

assay_context.cell_type_or_line: blood basophils from allergic rhinitis patients

spans.quote:
FcεRI, CD63, and CD203c expression on blood basophils induced by stimulant were measured at baseline and at 12 weeks after omalizumab treatment using flow cytometry.

Results

The RQLQ score in OMA-AR/NB decreased from 33.0 ± 11.0 at baseline to 5.2 ± 4.2 at 12 weeks, while in OMA-AR/B, the score decreased from 33.8 ± 7.6 at baseline to 19.4 ± 5.9 at 12 weeks.

evidence.claim: CD63 surface expression is used as an activation marker on RBL mast cells measured by flow cytometry. After alpha-gal antigen stimulation, CD63+ cells increase ~3-fold compared to control-sensitized cells, confirming activation-induced surface translocation of CD63 in mast cells.

spans.quote:
To assess effector cell activation, we measured cell surface expression of activation marker CD63 by flow cytometry and mediator release through β-hexosaminidase release assays.

Results

After alpha-gal antigen stimulation, the percentage of CD63+ alpha-gal knockout RBL SX-38 cells sensitized with AGS sera increased 3-fold compared with cells sensitized with control serum. Select human AGS IgE clones facilitated alpha-gal antigen-dependent and antigen-independent CD63 upregulation.

evidence.claim: In a T2DM mouse model, flow cytometry reveals elevated platelet surface expression of CD63 (alongside CD62P and CD40L), indicating that CD63 is present on the platelet surface in a disease-state-dependent manner. DHM treatment significantly reduces platelet surface CD63, demonstrating pharmacological modulation of platelet CD63 surface levels.

spans.quote: A T2DM mouse model was established by feeding a high-fat diet (HFD) combined with streptozotocin (STZ) injection, followed by dietary supplementation with DHM (500 or 1000 mg kg<sup>-1</sup> in diets) for eight weeks. Flow cytometric analysis revealed that DHM significantly reduced platelet surface expression of CD62P, CD63, and CD40 ligands, decreased integrin αIIbβ3 activation, and suppressed intraplatelet reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. The exaggerated platelet aggregation and ATP secretion induced by thrombin and collagen were also markedly attenuated.

evidence.claim: CD63 is listed as a neutrophil surface marker measured by flow cytometry in a surgical cohort study (ONCAB vs OPCAB patients), establishing CD63 as a detectable surface marker on primary human neutrophils in a perioperative/inflammatory context.

assay_context.cell_type_or_line: peripheral blood neutrophils from cardiac surgery patients

spans.quote:
Secondary outcomes included monocyte Human leukocyte antigen-DR (HLA-DR) expression, lymphocyte programmed cell death protein-1 (PD-1) expression, and neutrophil surface markers (CD11b, CD18, CXCR2, CD35, CD63, CD66b, CD88, and programmed cell death-ligand 1). Neutrophil apoptosis, reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, and plasma inflammatory mediators (interleukin-6, tumor necrosis factor-alpha, interleukin-10) were also measured. Postoperative clinical outcomes and laboratory parameters were recorded.

Results

Data from 36 ONCAB patients and 18 OPCAB patients were analyzed.

evidence.claim: CD63 is used as a degranulation marker on tear polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs) from the ocular surface, measured by flow cytometry. More tear leukocytes are collected after sleep in participants with ocular allergy vs. healthy controls, with CD63 serving as a surface degranulation readout on these cells.

assay_context.cell_type_or_line: tear leukocytes / PMNs from ocular surface

spans.quote:
Samples were stained with antibodies against degranulation markers (CD66b, CD63), adhesion markers (CD11b, CD54), eosinophil marker (CD193), and aging marker (CD184), and analysed by flow cytometry.

Results

Significantly more tear leukocytes were collected after a night of sleep from participants with ocular allergy compared to healthy participants (p = 0.024), while there was no difference in late afternoon collections.

evidence.claim: HIV-exposed macrophages show upregulation of tetraspanins including CD63 on their surface, alongside ICAM-1/LFA-1, in a cell-state-induced manner following contact with HIV-infected T cells. This indicates that CD63 surface levels on macrophages are modulated by HIV exposure.

spans.quote: HIV-exposed macrophages showed inflammasome-linked death and IL-1β induction; contact enhanced Mf-T conjugates and upregulated ICAM-1/LFA-1 and tetraspanins.

evidence.claim: TIMP1 engages CD63 on the surface of macrophages (in conjunction with β1-integrin), activating AKT/mTOR signaling and stabilizing the M2 phenotype. This functional engagement confirms CD63 surface accessibility on macrophages and its role in macrophage polarization in the context of colorectal cancer liver metastasis.

spans.quote:
Mechanistically, TIMP1 engaged CD63/β1-integrin on macrophages, activating AKT/mTOR signaling and stabilizing the M2 phenotype.

Conclusions

CRC-derived TIMP1 remodels liver macrophages via the CD63/β1-integrin-AKT/mTOR pathway to promote a hepatic pre-metastatic niche.

evidence.claim: CD63 is identified as a conserved T-cell host factor supporting ACE2-independent SARS-CoV-2 entry in T lymphocytes, which express little to no ACE2. This establishes CD63 expression and surface accessibility in T cells as functionally relevant in the context of SARS-CoV-2 (Omicron) infection.

spans.quote:
Background

Severe Omicron cases present profound lymphocytopenia, suggesting variant-specific immune injury.

Results

We identify CD63 as a conserved T-cell host factor supporting ACE2-independent SARS-CoV-2 entry.

evidence.claim: Chronic wood smoke (WS) exposure in rats induces markedly increased CD63 expression in alveolar tissue, as detected by immunostaining, accompanied by increased exosome particle number in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid. CD63 is also elevated in alveolar regions of COPD patient lungs, indicating disease-state-induced upregulation of CD63 in alveolar epithelial/macrophage compartments.

spans.quote: Here, we show that chronic WS exposure in rats induces emphysematous lesions accompanied by markedly increased exosome release, reflected by elevated CD63 expression in alveoli and increased exosome particle number in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid.

evidence.claim: Astrocyte-specific GFP-tagged CD63 expression is robustly detected in brain and spinal cord following tamoxifen induction in a GFAP-CreERT2 × CD63-emGFP mouse model, establishing CD63 expression in astrocytes in vivo. Ischemic stroke significantly increases astrocyte-derived CD63+ small EVs in the ipsilesional hemisphere and spinal cord, demonstrating disease-state-induced upregulation of CD63-positive EV release from astrocytes.

assay_context.cell_type_or_line: astrocytes in brain and spinal cord

spans.quote:
The mouse line was generated by crossing GFAP-CreERT2 mice with CD63-emGFPloxP/stop/loxP mice. This system enables Tamoxifen-inducible, astrocyte-specific expression of GFP-tagged CD63, a tetraspanin enriched in sEVs. The model allows visualization and quantification of astrocyte-derived CD63-positive sEVs in vivo.

Results

Following Tamoxifen induction, GFP expression was robustly detected in the brain and spinal cord.

evidence.claim: In hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells, CD63 protein levels are regulated post-translationally via lysosome/autophagy-dependent turnover. ANXA2 loss reduces CD63 protein without affecting CD63 mRNA, and lysosomal acidification blockade (bafilomycin A1) rescues CD63 levels. This indicates that in HCC cells, CD63 protein abundance is controlled by lysosomal degradation, with implications for CD63 surface and exosomal availability.

spans.quote: ANXA2 loss reduces CD63 protein levels without a corresponding decrease in CD63 mRNA and is accompanied by activation of lysosome/autophagy-associated programs.

evidence.claim: CD63 predominantly localizes to multivesicular bodies (MVBs) in human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells (hUCMSCs), which are the primary precursors of extracellular vesicles. This intracellular MVB localization is the dominant subcellular compartment for CD63 in this cell type, consistent with its known lysosomal/late endosomal distribution.

assay_context.cell_type_or_line: human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells (hUCMSCs)

spans.quote: Given the predominant localization of CD63 to MVBs, which are the primary precursors of EVs, these findings suggest that H89 may modulate EV secretion pathways in hUCMSCs.

evidence.claim: Cellular protein expression of CD63 (along with CD9 and CD81) in skeletal muscle myocytes, white adipocytes, brown adipocytes, endothelial cells, and hepatocytes predicts the abundance of tetraspanin-expressing EVs secreted from those same cells, establishing differential CD63 expression across these cell types as a determinant of EV output.

assay_context.cell_type_or_line: skeletal muscle myocytes, adipocytes, endothelial cells, hepatocytes

spans.quote: For example, Garcia-Martin et al. compared cultured skeletal muscle (SkM) myocytes, white adipocytes, brown adipocytes, endothelial cells, and hepatocytes and found that cellular protein expression of the tetraspanins CD9, CD63, and CD81 predicts the abundance of tetraspanin-expressing EVs secreted from those same cells. 2 Similarly, our group has shown that expression of genes encoding EV secretion machinery is greater in human SkM cells and tissues than white adipocytes, and mouse SkM secretes ∼100× more EVs than the same mass of white adipose tissue ex vivo .

evidence.claim: Single-cell RNA-seq atlas analysis shows that the highest overall expression of EV-related genes (including tetraspanins such as CD63) occurs in secretory cells of the pancreas and in multiple non-neuronal cell populations of the brain, indicating cell-type-specific enrichment of CD63 expression in these tissues.

assay_context.cell_type_or_line: pancreatic secretory cells and brain non-neuronal cells

spans.quote: The highest overall expression of EV genes occurs in secretory cells of the pancreas and perhaps more surprisingly, multiple non-neuronal cell populations of the brain.

evidence.claim: EVs from Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC) patients are enriched for endolysosomal proteins CD63 and LAMP1, as revealed by multiplexed EV immunoassays and direct stochastic imaging. This enrichment in NPC patient CSF and dermal fibroblast-derived EVs reflects the endolysosomal compartment origin of CD63 and its disease-state-dependent EV loading.

assay_context.cell_type_or_line: CSF and dermal fibroblasts from NPC patients

spans.quote: Direct stochastic imaging and multiplexed EV immunoassays revealed that NPC EVs were enriched for endolysosomal proteins (CD63, Lamp1).
